Revenue leaks at the hand-offs

Most cross-functional loss is not dramatic. It appears as waiting, missing context, repeated work and decisions that nobody explicitly owns.

RevOpHubs field guide · Published September 2026 · Updated 1 October 2026

Inside each function, the work may appear healthy. Marketing delivers leads. Sales accepts them. Customer success receives the signed customer. Yet the customer experiences one journey, not the organisation chart. Every transition between teams creates a moment where context, time and accountability can disappear.

A hand-off is a decision, not a notification

Many processes define a hand-off as the moment a record changes owner or a notification is sent. That describes system activity. A real hand-off is complete only when the receiving team has the information, authority and capacity to perform the next work.

That requires four elements: an explicit trigger, required context, a named receiving owner and a confirmation that the work has been accepted. Without these, the sender believes the work moved while the receiver still needs to interpret or reconstruct it.

The most expensive hand-off is the one both teams believe the other team owns.

Look for failure demand

Failure demand is work created because the process did not work correctly the first time. It includes chasing missing information, re-qualifying a lead, correcting a contract detail, rebuilding a forecast category or explaining a promise that was never recorded.

These tasks are often invisible in dashboards because they occur in messages, meetings and private notes. Observe a sample of recent hand-offs and count the extra interactions required before the receiving team could act. The volume of rework is a direct measure of process quality.

The Revenue System Assessment compares process strength with the five layers around it.

Map one critical transition

Do not begin by documenting the entire customer lifecycle. Choose the hand-off with the strongest combination of volume, delay and commercial consequence. Map what happens now using actual records rather than the official process diagram.

For that transition, answer:

  • What observable event should trigger the hand-off?
  • Which information must be present and trustworthy?
  • Who accepts the work, and within what response time?
  • What happens when the criteria are not met?
  • Which measure shows whether the hand-off improved?

What should a marketing-to-sales hand-off include?

A marketing-to-sales hand-off should include a qualification trigger, the buyer's context, a named sales owner, a response deadline and an explicit acceptance or return decision. Changing a CRM owner alone does not confirm that sales can act.

A worked example: a buyer requests a demonstration

Illustrative example, not a client case or an industry benchmark. A B2B buyer requests a demonstration after reading a product guide. Marketing records the source, but the sales team receives only a name and an email address. The salesperson must reconstruct the request before deciding what to do.

The teams agree the following operating contract. The one-business-day deadline is a proposed starting point for this example; set your own target using coverage, buyer expectations and observed response times.

  1. Trigger: a buyer requests a demonstration and the company meets the agreed account-fit criteria. A content download alone does not trigger this route.
  2. Required context: company, contact details supplied by the buyer, request, product or use case of interest, source and relevant previous interactions. Record unknown information as unknown; do not invent budget or buying authority.
  3. Owner: route the record to a named salesperson using the agreed territory or account rules. Keep a named queue owner for cases that cannot be assigned.
  4. Acceptance: within one business day, the salesperson records either acceptance with a next action and due date, or return with a specific reason. Acceptance is a workflow decision; it does not automatically create a qualified opportunity.
  5. Exception: return an incomplete record to a named marketing owner with the missing field and a due date. Escalate an overdue decision to the sales manager. Keep the buyer informed while the teams resolve the exception.

The CRM needs to make that agreement visible: hand-off time, receiving owner, decision time, decision reason and next action. These can be properties, statuses or tasks in your existing CRM. Agree their meaning before configuring the workflow.

How do you measure whether a hand-off improved?

Take a baseline from recent records, then compare the same transition after the change. Keep the segment, observation period and qualification rules consistent; a small sample can reveal failure patterns but does not establish a company-wide revenue impact.

  • Acceptance rate: accepted hand-offs divided by all hand-offs in the selected cohort. Report returned and still-pending records separately.
  • Decision time: elapsed time from the trigger to acceptance or return. Track the median and the oldest pending records. State whether you use business hours or calendar hours.
  • Completeness rate: records with every agreed required field present at hand-off divided by all hand-offs. Check accuracy separately; a filled field may still be wrong.
  • Rework rate: hand-offs requiring clarification or correction before work can start divided by all hand-offs. Use reason codes to identify the recurring causes.
  • Commercial progression: accepted hand-offs that reach the agreed next meaningful stage within a defined follow-up window divided by accepted hand-offs with that full observation window. Faster acceptance alone does not establish better conversion.

Run a two-week hand-off audit

Week one: the marketing and sales process owners review a manageable sample of recent demonstration requests, including returned and pending records. Trace the trigger, context, owner, decision and next action. Identify one recurring failure and agree the contract above for that transition.

Week two: pilot the contract, record exceptions and review the baseline measures together. The deliverable is a one-page hand-off agreement, an exception log and a decision on which stable rules to automate. Continue observing commercial progression beyond the pilot where the sales cycle requires it.

For a broader diagnosis, use the Revenue System Assessment. If the agreement is clear but the CRM cannot represent it, work through the CRM Readiness Check before redesigning the system.

Automation comes after agreement

It is tempting to solve a slow hand-off with routing rules and alerts. Automation is useful when the rules are stable and exceptions are understood. When teams disagree about criteria or ownership, automation removes the conversation without resolving the disagreement.

First establish the operational contract between sender and receiver. Test it manually for a short period. Observe exceptions. Then automate the stable parts and preserve a visible route for cases that require judgement.

Review the customer consequence

An internal process can appear efficient while creating a poor customer experience. A fast sales-to-onboarding hand-off is not successful if the customer has to repeat the context, objectives and concerns already discussed during the sale.

Include the customer consequence in the hand-off measure: time to first value, repeated questions, expectation gaps and early support demand. This keeps optimisation connected to revenue rather than administrative speed alone.
